title: Korea’s unanimous hold left the next hike contingent on who shared in the chip boom
summary: The Bank of Korea held its Base Rate at 3.00% on 22 October after two consecutive increases. All members supported the hold. The minutes released on 10 November show why that consensus is a poor guide to the next decision. Members saw higher exports and an inflation rate above target, yet the effects of the earlier hikes were already visible in market rates and the won. A further increase would reach indebted households and small businesses well before anyone could establish how much semiconductor income would reach them. The issue dividing the assessments was how much more restraint would be needed as those two processes unfolded. No member attached a date or probability to the next hike (pp. 1–5, 8–12).

The export shock raised both output and Korea’s purchasing power. AI investment abroad supported chip shipments, while rising semiconductor prices improved the terms of trade and lifted nominal corporate income. Equipment investment and related construction benefited directly. One member anticipated growth above the August projections in both 2026 and 2027, with a positive output gap in prospect. An improvement in tax receipts and active fiscal policy could spread the gain beyond the exporters. Another member emphasised that consumption and employment had received only a gradual lift. A third stressed the combination of expensive credit and high prices facing sectors outside the boom. A national growth revision could therefore justify either earlier restraint or more patience, depending on where the additional income was being spent (pp. 2–8).

Members also questioned how persistent the income gain would prove. Higher long yields abroad increased the hurdle for AI investments whose profitability was already under scrutiny. Korean equity prices had corrected amid those concerns and tougher competition in chips. An export industry could still be expanding production while investors marked down the value of its future earnings. Heavy sector concentration therefore exposed domestic markets, the currency and the real economy to the same adverse revision in expectations. One member called for work on the distributional as well as the aggregate consequences. Another contrasted weak service-sector productivity and high delinquencies among vulnerable borrowers with strong headline growth. The latter saw a temporary fiscal opportunity to finance structural improvements, while warning that spending directed chiefly at consumption could add to inflation (pp. 4–7, 10–11).

Inflation justified vigilance even after its September decline. Headline prices were 2.9% higher than a year earlier and core prices 2.8% higher, both above the 2% target. Temporary August influences complicated the comparison. One member saw signs of acceleration underneath the fall, especially in durable goods. Another highlighted pressure in personal services as well. Oil and disruptions to refined products raised costs, and dearer chips were feeding into IT prices. Against that, a stronger won reduced the local-currency cost of imports. A fourth member put the exchange rate in the region of 1,330 won per dollar. Members cited the current-account surplus, dollar sales and prior tightening as possible explanations for appreciation despite broad US dollar strength. The exchange rate offered some relief, but could change direction if global risk appetite deteriorated (pp. 3, 7–11).

Domestic bond, equity and housing markets were sending different signals. Members described an initial rise in Korean government yields alongside foreign yields. Domestic fiscal conditions and measures affecting Treasury bond supply and demand subsequently unwound much of the rise in one account. Another member reported little change in corporate credit spreads. Foreign yield pressure itself had several candidate drivers, including inflation, concern about public finances and heavy borrowing by large AI investors. The reported expectation of another Fed increase was the fifth member’s account of market expectations following the September US meeting. It supplied neither a price for the next Korean decision nor a measure of any surprise when these minutes appeared (pp. 8–11).

Housing made the cost of waiting less straightforward. Total household lending declined in September, but non-housing loans accounted for the fall while housing-related lending continued to rise. Members pointed to seasonal effects and reduced individual equity trading as partial explanations for the weakness in other credit. They described different aspects of capital-region housing. Some noted renewed acceleration or widening gains, while another saw some moderation after government measures and earlier rate increases, alongside sharp increases in specific locations. Strong mortgage demand and high arrears among vulnerable borrowers could thus coexist. A policy decision based on aggregate household credit alone would miss both (pp. 3, 6, 8, 10–12).

Across six unattributed accounts, the common reason to wait was the lag between action and transmission. The first account emphasised testing whether export-led gains would sustain core inflation. The second placed greater weight on sectors left behind. The third stressed the fiscal mix and vulnerable borrowers. The fourth judged that financial conditions had tightened enough to give households and firms time to adjust. The fifth saw domestic conditions evolving broadly within the expected range while overseas rates and geopolitical risks remained uncertain. The sixth still favoured a restrictive stance and a conditional assessment of the pace of any further increases. The document supports a directional reading of the debate: further tightening remained a live option. It supplies no collective forward commitment or named distribution of future votes.

questions.question: How much semiconductor income was reaching consumers outside the export sector?
questions.detail: If additional income remained in retained corporate profits and equipment orders, strong GDP could coexist with soft domestic pricing. If it reached wages, dividends and consumption quickly, the case for another increase strengthened. Compare the Bank’s sectoral national accounts, household income and consumption releases, wage settlements and domestic orders available around the November forecast.

questions.question: How persistent was the underlying rise in prices after currency appreciation?
questions.detail: A weaker dollar import bill could conceal stronger pricing in services or IT goods. A rates investor needs to know which force would survive a reversal in the won. Match import prices in contract currency and won with detailed consumer prices, monthly momentum and the Bank’s contemporaneous inflation assessment.

questions.question: Who was borrowing against housing while aggregate household credit fell?
questions.detail: The financial-stability consequences depend on borrower leverage, location and refinancing dates. Compare Seoul-area transaction volumes and mortgage originations with bank delinquency disclosures, separating housing credit from seasonal and securities-related loans. That would show whether a further hike would chiefly restrain new demand or intensify existing cash-flow stress.

questions.question: How much of the sovereign yield move reflected Korean policy expectations?
questions.detail: The minutes give competing domestic supply and international-rate explanations for the observed reversal. To gauge curve exposure, consult contemporaneous Treasury issuance announcements, dealer commentary and time-stamped Korean money-market and government-bond quotes around the decision and the later minutes release separately.

limitation: The Bank describes this English publication as an excerpt. Its 13 PDF pages include the attendance list and six unattributed accounts of members’ views. It gives unanimous support for the October decision but no speaker-by-speaker forward votes or intraday pricing.
